lines.trans: Kostya, it seems Vika loves me!
Great! Or is it?
Damn, Kostya, this is a dangerous situation.
If she loves me, a relationship is needed.
And what is bad about a relationship?
Then a wedding, and then kids!
Why do I need all of this right now?
You are simply afraid of adult life.
I love freedom and adventures!
Vika is a mature and smart girl.
She will not tolerate your nonsense.
Exactly, she will start educating me.
Then talk to her honestly.
No, better that I keep quiet.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('so, and what about') (starting a question: а жвачку?) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'pancake', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Тогда положите мне ещё парочку блинов!
examples.trans: Then serve me a couple more pancakes!

examples.text: Большое спасибо вам за вкусные блины.
examples.trans: Thank you very much for the delicious pancakes.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to be afraid'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense. The reflexive suffix '-ся'/'-сь' makes the action intransitive, reciprocal, or directed at the subject.

examples.trans: We have nobody to fear here.

examples.text: Это наш город. Нам здесь бояться некого.
examples.trans: This is our town. We have nobody to fear here.

meanings.note: the present tense is normally left out: я мэр = I am the mayor
Secondary conversational sense ('there is, there are') (present есть; у меня есть = I have) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
future: буду / будешь ... + infinitive

examples.trans: You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

взрослый.gloss: adult, grown-up; (as a noun) a grown-up

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'adult', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.
as a noun, often plural: взрослые = grown-ups

examples.text: Маленькие умеют терпеть, а взрослые нет, понял?
examples.trans: Little ones can hold on, but grown-ups can't, got it?

meanings.en: to bring up, to raise (a child)
meanings.note: Prefix 'во-' ('into, up') marks inward or upward movement (stem 'спитывать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to bring up, to raise', paired with 'воспитать'.

examples.text: Марина, преподаватель. Разведена, воспитывает больного ребёнка.
examples.trans: Marina, a lecturer. Divorced, raising a sick child.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('here') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or discourse tone in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('! = you'll see!') (emphasis) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: All right, here you go. There, look.

meanings.note: ends a conversation or an order: 'Всё, свободен' = that's all, you can go
Secondary conversational sense ('that's it, done') (at the start of a sentence) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: Abstract feminine noun formed with the productive Slavic suffix '-ость', denoting the quality or state of 'nonsense'.
Secondary conversational sense ('stupidity, foolishness') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Что за глупости? Значит, Осипенко сам эти деньги украл!
examples.trans: What nonsense? That means Osipenko stole that money himself!

meanings.note: Derived feminine noun formed with a productive Slavic suffix, used in spoken Russian to mean 'girl'.

examples.text: Девушки, как я, у тебя не будет!
examples.trans: You'll never have a girl like me!

держаться.gloss: to hold on; to stick with

meanings.note: за + accusative: держись за руку = hold on to my hand

meanings.en: to stick with, keep close to
meanings.note: + genitive: держитесь меня = stick with me
Secondary conversational sense ('to hang in there') (держись! = hang in there!) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Держитесь меня, и всё будет хорошо.
examples.trans: Stick with me and everything will be fine.

examples.text: Держитесь меня, и всё у вас будет хорошо. Потому что я кто?
examples.trans: Stick with me, and everything will be fine for you. Because who am I?

examples.text: Держись, друг, до конца этой тяжёлой смены остался час!
examples.trans: Hang in there, my friend, there is one hour left until the end of this tough shift!

meanings.note: condition: если хочешь = if you want; а если нет? = and if not?
Common feminine noun meaning 'life' in everyday Russian.
Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'what for'.

examples.trans: Oh, Samson. What have you come for?

meanings.note: emphasis: вот поэтому ты и... = that's exactly why you...

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'or', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.
вот именно = that's just it, quite right
Secondary conversational sense ('namely') (а именно = namely) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Именно это я и хотел сказать.
examples.trans: That is justamente what I wanted to say.

examples.text: Вот именно. Но мне сдаваться нельзя.
examples.trans: Exactly. But I must not give up.

meanings.note: мне кажется = I think, it seems to me
Secondary conversational sense ('it seems, I think') (кажется as a parenthetical word) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I think I've seen you somewhere.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'class', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('classroom') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('cool!, great!') (colloquial exclamation) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Вот это настоящий высший класс кулинарного искусства!
examples.trans: Now that is true top class in culinary art!

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'better'.
Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to love, to like', paired with 'полюбить'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to like') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

молчать.gloss: to be silent, to say nothing

meanings.en: to be silent, to keep quiet
meanings.note: почему ты молчишь? = why aren't you saying anything?

examples.text: Ну что ты молчишь? Ты толстый, ты не спортсмен!
examples.trans: Well, why are you so quiet? You're fat, you're no athlete!

examples.text: Молчи лучше, пока шеф не заметил нашу ошибку!
examples.trans: Better keep quiet before the chef notices our mistake!

meanings.en: must, need to, it is necessary
meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'it is necessary'.

examples.trans: We need to do even more.

meanings.note: + imperfective infinitive or + accusative

examples.text: Это хорошо, что готово. А то мы уже начали беспокоиться.
examples.trans: It's good that it's ready. We were starting to worry.

examples.text: Ну что, коллеги, давайте начнём наше утреннее совещание!
examples.trans: Well then, colleagues, let us begin our morning meeting!

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates
+ genitive: 'у нас нет выбора' = we have no choice
Secondary conversational sense ('there isn't') (+ genitive) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
short form 'нужен / нужна / нужно / нужны' + dative: 'мне нужна работа' = I need a job
High-frequency Russian pronoun ('she') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: Паша, я больше не хочу о ней слышать. Понял?
examples.trans: Pasha, I don't want to hear about her again. Understood?

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('dangerous').

examples.trans: This is a very dangerous job.

examples.text: У меня много опасных друзей. А иначе я позвоню ребятам.
examples.trans: I have many dangerous friends. Otherwise I'll call the guys.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'from' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('of') (тошнит от = sick of) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: Verbal action or result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание', meaning 'attitude' in conversational and formal Russian.
Secondary conversational sense ('attitude, treatment') (towards someone or something) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: А я испорчу отношения с будущим мэром.
examples.trans: And I'll ruin my relationship with the future mayor.
We have a very warm relationship.

examples.text: Ты с ума сошёл? У нас с тобой только деловые отношения!
examples.trans: Have you lost your mind? Between you and me it's strictly business!

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('bad').

examples.text: Я вчера ел маринованные грибы. Может, один гриб был плохой.
examples.trans: Yesterday I ate pickled mushrooms. Maybe one mushroom was bad.

meanings.en: to have a talk, to speak (with someone)
meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'говорить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to have a talk', forming an aspectual pair with 'говорить'.

examples.text: Поговори с Аракеляном. Пусть он заберёт заявление.
examples.trans: Talk to Arakelyan. Get him to withdraw his statement.

meanings.note: comparative of далеко with prefix по-

examples.trans: Stand a little further back behind the pines.
Step a little further away from the fire.

examples.text: Иван, встань подальше, вон там за соснами.
examples.trans: Ivan, stand further back, over there behind the pines.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'then'.
Verbal action or result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание', meaning 'adventure' in conversational and formal Russian.

examples.trans: The main adventure is only just beginning!

examples.text: В Москве Макса ждали новые приключения.
examples.trans: New adventures awaited Max in Moscow.

examples.text: И главное приключение ещё только начинается!
examples.trans: And the main adventure is only just beginning!

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'just'.
Secondary conversational sense ('easy') (это просто = it's easy) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: Derived masculine noun formed with a productive Slavic suffix, used in spoken Russian to mean 'child'.
+ instrumental; со before some consonant clusters: со всеми

examples.trans: Share it all equally with everyone, understand?

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'wedding', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: Watch the movie Wedding on Skype.

examples.text: Макс, зачем ты соврал про нашу будущую свадьбу?
examples.trans: Max, why did you lie about our future wedding?
Then a wedding, and then kids!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'вобода'). Common feminine noun meaning 'freedom, liberty' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Right now there's freedom, cars, the sea!
He was released (came out to freedom).

examples.text: Ну выйдешь ты через десять лет, и что? А сейчас свобода, машины, море!
examples.trans: Well, you'll get out in ten years, and then what? Right now there's freedom, cars, the sea!

meanings.note: 'сейчас буду' = I'll be right there
Secondary conversational sense ('in a moment') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: Borrowed via French/German from Medieval Latin 'situatio' (position, state of affairs, from 'situs').

examples.trans: This is a very complicated situation.

examples.text: Да никуда я не пряталась! Я контролировала ситуацию.
examples.trans: I wasn't hiding anywhere! I was controlling the situation.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('your') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.

examples.text: Я бы на твоём месте подумал.
examples.trans: If I were you, I'd think about it.

терпеть.gloss: to bear, to put up with; to hold on

meanings.en: to put up with, to bear
meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to bear', forming an aspectual pair with 'потерпеть'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('to hold on, to wait') (e.g. to wait for the toilet) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Маленькие умеют терпеть, а взрослые нет, понял?
examples.trans: Little ones can hold on, but grown-ups can't, got it?

related.gloss: to be patient for a while

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'then'.
Secondary conversational sense ('then, in that case') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я тебе тогда сказал: ты меня ещё поцелуешь.
examples.trans: I told you back then: you'll kiss me one day.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'мный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('clever, smart').

examples.text: Ты же у нас такая умная!
Ты же у нас такая умная! Скажи, что сделать, я сделаю.
examples.trans: You're the clever one here! Tell me what to do, and I'll do it.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Do you want me to tell you honestly?

examples.text: Всё честно, Лёха. Взрослые не умеют ждать.
examples.trans: It's all fair, Lyokha. Grown-ups can't wait.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('that') (conjunction) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('? = well?') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: pointing at a thing or a situation; 'это' + noun = 'this is ...'
points at something: это моё = that's mine
Secondary conversational sense ('is') (linking word: главное — это народ) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
